title: Qualifying life events
summary: Defines qualifying life events, how they open a special enrollment period, deadlines, documentation and what to do if you do not qualify.

assets.alt: Family on couch (qualifying life events page banner)

atoms.title: What a qualifying life event is
atoms.question: What is a qualifying life event for health insurance?
atoms.text: A qualifying life event is a life-changing situation, sometimes planned and sometimes unexpected, that can affect you and your health insurance. Experiencing a significant life change may allow you to change your health plan outside of the annual enrollment period, also called open enrollment. If you have had one, check your plan materials, contact your employer or call the number on your member ID card.
questions: What counts as a qualifying life event?
Can I change my health insurance after a big life change?

atoms.title: Common qualifying life events
atoms.question: What events count as qualifying life events?
atoms.text: Qualifying life events include, but are not necessarily limited to: getting married, getting divorced, having or adopting a baby, the death of someone who shares your health plan, moving to a new area, earning U.S. citizenship, turning 26, turning 65, experiencing a shift in employment status, and loss of health insurance.

Is turning 26 a qualifying life event?
Does losing my job count as a qualifying life event?

atoms.title: How to qualify for a special enrollment period
atoms.question: How do I qualify for a special enrollment period?
atoms.text: If you experience any qualifying life event, you qualify for a special enrollment period (SEP), which means you can enroll in a health plan outside the annual enrollment period. Sometimes SEPs are offered for other qualifying reasons, such as natural disaster relief, pandemic relief or a public health emergency.

atoms.title: Losing Medicaid opens a special enrollment period
atoms.question: Do I get a special enrollment period if I lose Medicaid?
atoms.text: If you are no longer eligible for Medicaid, you qualify for a special enrollment period (SEP). If you are asked to renew or recertify your Medicaid (also called redetermination) and you lose your Medicaid coverage, you may qualify for a special enrollment period.

atoms.title: How to enroll after a qualifying life event
atoms.question: How do I enroll in a plan after a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: After a qualifying life event, check your plan materials, contact your employer or call the phone number on your member ID card. Three things to know: timing, because changes can most often be made within either 30 or 60 days after the event; the deadline, because missing it may mean waiting until the next open enrollment period; and documentation, because you may need to submit documents confirming the event.
questions: What do I do after a qualifying life event?
Do I need proof of a life event to change my plan?

atoms.title: 30 or 60 day window to make changes
atoms.question: How long do I have to change my plan after a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: Changes after a qualifying life event can most often be made either 30 or 60 days after the life event happens. If you miss this deadline, you may have to wait until the next open enrollment period, which could be as long as a year.
questions: What is the deadline to enroll after getting married?
How many days after a life event can I change health insurance?

atoms.title: Turning 65 is a qualifying life event
atoms.question: Is turning 65 a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: Turning 65 is a qualifying life event. It gives you a chance to look into your opportunities to choose a Medicare plan. Parts A and B are sometimes called Original Medicare, and they do not cover everything: services like dental work, vision exams and eye care, and out-of-pocket costs such as deductibles are not covered.
questions: What should I do when I turn 65?

atoms.title: Medicare Parts C and D
atoms.question: What are Medicare Part C and Part D?
atoms.text: Medicare Part C, also called Medicare Advantage, is a private health plan that combines hospital and medical insurance, plus the potential for additional health benefits. Medicare Part D plans, offered by insurance companies approved by Medicare, add prescription drug coverage to Original Medicare and Medicare Supplement insurance plans.

atoms.title: Documents you may need for a life event
atoms.question: What documents do I need for a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: When you experience a qualifying life event, you may be asked for documents confirming it, and the type depends on the event. Events with common documentation lists include marriage, divorce or legal separation, adoption or birth of a child, a dependent passing away, losing or gaining eligibility for other health benefits, turning 26 and aging off a parent's plan, and moving out of or into a plan area. Ask your health insurance provider what is needed for your situation.

What paperwork do I need after turning 26?

atoms.title: Options without a special enrollment period
atoms.question: What if I don't qualify for a special enrollment period?
atoms.text: If you are between enrollment periods and have not had a qualifying life event, short term insurance can bridge the gap. Standard short term health insurance plans can fill a gap in coverage from 1 month to just under one year, depending on your state. TriTerm Medical is a special type of short term health insurance available in select states that offers coverage for nearly 3 years.

atoms.title: Other insurance options to explore
atoms.question: What other types of insurance can I explore?
atoms.text: Beyond a standard health plan, UnitedHealthcare points people to other options to explore: Individual & Family ACA Marketplace plans, student health insurance, fixed benefit health insurance, hospital insurance, term life insurance, critical illness insurance, international travel medical insurance and accident insurance.
